recommendations.source_detail: sql:long_idle_time ref=0 + agent_discovered ref=1: idle_ratio=0.995, vcore_utilization=0.015. The job is structurally sequential (300+ single-task stages from one callsite). Additional workers would sit idle for >99% of wall-clock time.
recommendations.rationale: The cluster currently has 1 worker and cluster_autoscaling=False. idle_ratio=0.995 and vcore_utilization=0.015 confirm the single executor is nearly entirely idle — not because it needs more parallelism, but because the driver dispatches one 1-task stage at a time and waits for each to complete before launching the next. Adding workers would not help; each stage has only 1 partition and 1 task, so only 1 executor core is ever used per stage. The correct action is to keep the cluster at its current minimum (1 worker) and avoid any scale-out that would waste cost on idle executors. This recommendation is defensive: it documents that the long_idle_time insight (ref=0) should NOT be addressed by adding capacity, and that the current single-worker configuration is already the right-sized baseline for this workload's architecture.
recommendations.explanation: The cluster currently runs with exactly 1 worker and cluster_autoscaling=False, and the telemetry confirms there is no utilisation headroom to exploit: vcore_utilization is 0.015 (1.5%) and idle_ratio is 0.995 (99.5%) across all 156 time-series buckets. Every stage dispatches exactly 1 task against 1 partition, so only 1 executor core is ever active at a time; additional workers would simply sit idle, burning cost. Setting clusterMaxWorkers=1 explicitly documents and enforces the ceiling so that if autoscaling is accidentally re-enabled in the future the platform cannot provision wasteful idle executors.
recommendations.expected_impact: Locks the cluster to its already-optimal single-worker footprint, preventing any inadvertent scale-out that would add idle executor cost without improving throughput.
recommendations.risk_note: If the upstream pipeline is later refactored to produce multi-partition stages, this hard cap of 1 will prevent horizontal scale-out and must be revisited alongside that architectural change.

recommendations.source_detail: sql:long_idle_time ref=0 + agent_discovered ref=1: Pair recommendation with clusterMaxWorkers to fully specify the scaling envelope on Databricks.
recommendations.rationale: On Databricks, both min and max cluster workers must be set together to define the executor scaling envelope. Min=1, Max=1 locks the cluster to a single worker, which is correct for a workload where every stage has exactly 1 task and 1 partition. Dynamic allocation is currently disabled (dynamic_allocation_enabled=False), so no additional platform machinery is needed. This explicitly prevents the autoscaler from spinning up idle workers if autoscaling is later re-enabled inadvertently.
recommendations.explanation: On Databricks, min and max worker counts must be configured together to form a valid scaling envelope; leaving both unset means the boundary is implicitly undefined. Because dynamic_allocation_enabled=False and every stage in this workload produces exactly 1 task, a min of 1 worker is the smallest valid value that matches the true compute requirement. Pairing clusterMinWorkers=1 with clusterMaxWorkers=1 explicitly locks the cluster to a single worker, which is consistent with the observed vcore_utilization of 0.015 and idle_ratio of 0.995 — the workload never needs more than one executor core simultaneously.
recommendations.expected_impact: Establishes a fully-defined, min=max=1 worker envelope that prevents the autoscaler from spinning up additional idle workers if autoscaling is re-enabled, and makes the intended single-worker configuration explicit and auditable.
recommendations.risk_note: Setting min equal to max effectively disables any future ability to scale out without a config change; ensure this intent is documented so on-call engineers do not accidentally increase only one of the two bounds.

recommendations.source_detail: agent_discovered insight ref=3: driver heap peaks at 82% utilization (1.175 GB of ~1.44 GB) with avg GC time of 1264 ms/bucket over 156 buckets. Default 1g heap is too small for managing 300+ sequential DAG metadata accumulations.
recommendations.rationale: The driver JVM is under sustained heap stress — not the executors. Driver heap peaks at 1.175 GB against a ~1.44 GB heap (82% utilization), and GC time averages 1264 ms per 8-minute bucket (peak 2284 ms/bucket) across 156 buckets (~20 hours). This is caused by the driver accumulating job metadata, event-bus payloads, and RDD lineage objects for each of the 300+ sequential single-task stages without releasing them promptly. The default spark.driver.memory is 1g; the effective heap (~1.44 GB with JVM overhead deducted) is being consistently pushed to its limit. A single step increase to 2g doubles the available heap space, giving the GC a comfortable working set and reducing stop-the-world pauses that contribute to the per-stage scheduling latency. This is explicitly a short-term mitigation until the stage-proliferation architectural issue (ref=1) is addressed. Step is conservative (1× current) and reversible.
recommendations.explanation: The pressure problem here sits on the driver, not the executors. Time-series data shows driver heap averaging 1.44 GB (min 1.435 GB, max 1.442 GB) across all 156 eight-minute buckets, with used heap peaking at 1.175 GB — an 82% utilisation of the ~1.44 GB effective heap that results from the 1 g default after JVM overhead deduction. Driver GC time averages 1,264 ms per bucket and peaks at 2,284 ms, indicating sustained stop-the-world pressure caused by the driver accumulating job metadata, event-bus payloads, and RDD lineage objects across 300+ sequential single-task stages without headroom to reclaim memory efficiently. Raising spark.driver.memory from the default 1g to 2g roughly doubles the available heap, giving the GC a comfortable working set and reducing the stop-the-world pauses that contribute to per-stage scheduling latency.
recommendations.expected_impact: Expected to materially reduce driver GC pause frequency and duration per stage, lowering per-stage scheduling overhead and shortening overall job wall-clock time while the underlying stage-proliferation architecture is addressed.
recommendations.risk_note: This is a short-term mitigation; if the number of sequential stages continues to grow, heap pressure will return at the higher memory setting, and the underlying cause — excessive single-task stage proliferation — must still be resolved architecturally.

unactioned_insights.title: Extreme Stage Proliferation: 300+ Sequential Single-Task Stages from One Code Callsite
unactioned_insights.description: The job executes over 298 fully serialized Spark stages (Stages 0–297+), every single one launched from IngestLander.scala:201 with exactly 1 task and 1 partition. Each stage incurs ~450 ms of scheduler overhead (task serialization, DAGScheduler round-trip, result fetch), adding at least 2+ minutes of pure overhead on top of actual execution. With idle_ratio=0.995 and vcore_utilization=0.015, the executor is nearly entirely idle — waiting for the driver to dispatch the next single-task stage. This is the structural root cause of the already-flagged long_idle_time. The job is architecturally a sequential for-loop implemented as 300 separate Spark actions rather than a single batched action.
unactioned_insights.reason: The root cause is a code-level architectural issue: IngestLander.scala:201 implements a sequential for-loop as 300+ separate Spark actions instead of a single batched action. This cannot be addressed via any Spark or cluster configuration parameter. The correct fix is a source-code refactor (batch multiple DataFrames into a single union+write, or move the loop to a driver-only Delta API call). No valid config_key from the allowed list can resolve stage proliferation.

unactioned_insights.title: Duration Hard-Plateau at ~173,000s Across 7 Consecutive Runs — Structural, Not Data-Volume Driven
unactioned_insights.description: The task duration jumped from 15k s to 173k s between historical runs 1–2 and has been pinned at exactly ~173k s (±200s) for runs 3–9, a plateau lasting at least 7 runs. This is not a data-growth trend — a gradual growth would show variance. The cliff-edge onset and tight plateau suggest the number of stages/tables processed by IngestLander was increased at a specific deployment date and has not changed since. The current run's shorter duration (74.5k s) is not an improvement — it is a reduced run (22nd percentile), possibly processing fewer source partitions than normal. The 173k s plateau represents a fixed structural ceiling unless the stage count is reduced.
unactioned_insights.reason: The duration hard-plateau at ~173,000s is a downstream symptom of the stage-proliferation architectural issue (ref=1). The plateau will dissolve if and only if the stage count is reduced through code changes. No configuration parameter can change the number of Spark stages dispatched by the application. Additionally, the current run's reduced duration (74.5k s, 22nd percentile) warrants investigation at the data/orchestration layer to confirm dataset completeness — this is also not addressable via config.

agent_insights.identifier: Extreme Stage Proliferation: 300+ Sequential Single-Task Stages from One Code Callsite
agent_insights.title: Extreme Stage Proliferation: 300+ Sequential Single-Task Stages from One Code Callsite
agent_insights.description: The job executes over 298 fully serialized Spark stages (Stages 0–297+), every single one launched from IngestLander.scala:201 with exactly 1 task and 1 partition. Each stage incurs ~450 ms of scheduler overhead (task serialization, DAGScheduler round-trip, result fetch), adding at least 2+ minutes of pure overhead on top of actual execution. With idle_ratio=0.995 and vcore_utilization=0.015, the executor is nearly entirely idle — waiting for the driver to dispatch the next single-task stage. This is the structural root cause of the already-flagged long_idle_time. The job is architecturally a sequential for-loop implemented as 300 separate Spark actions rather than a single batched action.
agent_insights.evidence: Events show Stages 0–297 each with numTasks=1 and partitions=1, all sourced from IngestLander.scala:201. Stage start-to-start gap is ~450ms per stage (e.g., Stage 0: 1781457948–1781458007, Stage 1: 1781458007–1781458012). idle_ratio=0.995, vcore_utilization=0.015, executor_cores=2 but only 1 vcore ever used (vcores_max_used_over_time avg=0.83). Pipeline duration=74520s vs total Spark stage execution time of ~10s (all stages combined).
agent_insights.suggested_action: Refactor IngestLander.scala:201 to batch multiple landing outputs into a single Spark action (e.g., union all target DataFrames and write once, or use a multi-table write). If sequential isolation is required by design (e.g., each stage writes to a different Delta table), consider whether Spark is the right execution engine for this loop — a driver-only loop using the Delta API directly would eliminate executor idle cost entirely.

agent_insights.identifier: Driver-Side JVM GC Pressure — Inverted from Typical Pattern
agent_insights.title: Driver-Side JVM GC Pressure — Inverted from Typical Pattern
agent_insights.description: The driver JVM GC time averages 1264 ms per 8-minute bucket (avg over 156 buckets) and peaks at 2284 ms/bucket, while executor GC pressure is near zero (gc_pressure=0.019). This is inverted from the typical over-provisioned-memory pattern. The driver is under heap stress from managing the metadata of 300+ sequential DAGs — each stage dispatch retains job metadata, event bus payloads, and RDD lineage in driver heap. This is not a memory-sizing issue but a design issue: the driver accumulates GC pressure monotonically as it loops through each sequential stage.
agent_insights.evidence: time_series_summary: driver_jvm_gc_time_over_time avg=1264 ms/bucket, max=2284 ms/bucket, over 156 buckets (20.8 hours). executor gc_pressure=0.019 (benign). driver_used_heap_memory avg=0.963 GB, max=1.175 GB (of ~1.44 GB heap — 82% utilization at peak). Active tasks avg=1075, but vcores_avg_used=0.058 — driver is the bottleneck, not the executor.
agent_insights.suggested_action: If the stage-proliferation refactor is not immediately feasible, increase driver memory on the m7gd.large instance as a short-term mitigation (driver heap is ~1.44 GB and peaks at 82% utilization). More importantly, reducing the stage count via batching will directly eliminate driver GC accumulation. Optionally, call SparkContext.cleaner or trigger checkpoint/unpersist between logical batches if isolation must be maintained.

triage_result.reasoning: All three health-gate thresholds that would force a Tier 1 classification are clear: retried_task_waste=0.0, gc_pressure=0.019 (executor-side, well below 0.20), has_spill=false, memory_headroom=0.66, and no failed task runs. The driver-side GC noted in insight 3 is real but is a symptom of the architectural loop problem, not an independent heap-sizing emergency — executor gc_pressure is the metric that drives Tier 1 GC classification and it is fine. Therefore no Tier 1 triggers fire. Insight 0 (long_idle_time) maps directly to the Tier 2 rule: idle_ratio=0.995, vcore_utilization=0.015 — the cluster is massively over-provisioned relative to actual parallelism; the single-worker cluster is paid for but almost entirely idle. Insight 1 (extreme stage proliferation) is the structural root cause of that idle time and the architectural bottleneck driving it; it falls under Tier 2 as the deeper explanation of the orphaned/idle-node pattern (the executor sits idle between each sequential single-task stage dispatch). Insight 2 (duration hard-plateau) is a historical trend / structural sizing observation — it informs how the stage count was fixed at a deployment boundary and that the current run is a reduced run, which is context for right-sizing decisions; it belongs in Tier 2 alongside the idle-time and stage proliferation insights because it explains the cluster-level cost ceiling. Insight 3 (driver-side GC pressure) is caused by the same sequential-DAG loop design; it is not an executor memory or instance-type issue and does not independently trigger Tier 1. It is best classified as Tier 4 fine-tuning context (driver heap tuning / design feedback), since the fix is the same code restructuring already called out in insight 1, and no separate memory or instance-type change is warranted on its own. No cross-insight conflicts exist: there is no spill blocking a memory reduction, no skew+high-CPU blocking executor reduction, and AQE is not active. The recommendations are mutually reinforcing — fixing the sequential loop (insight 1) directly resolves idle time (insight 0), the plateau (insight 2), and driver GC pressure (insight 3).
